title: Convolution Theorem
body:
Convolution of two functions is

$$
(f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau)\,g(x - \tau)\,d\tau
$$

which reads as: flip $g$, slide it along $f$, and at each offset record the overlap. It is the
operation that describes **a signal passed through a filter**, or a probability distribution added
to another, or a blur applied to an image.

The theorem is one line and it is the most useful line in the course:

$$
\widehat{f * g} = \hat{f} \cdot \hat{g}
$$

**Convolution in one domain is pointwise multiplication in the other.** The messy sliding integral
becomes elementwise multiplication of two spectra. It runs the other way too: multiplying two
signals convolves their spectra, which is why modulation smears a spectrum out.

## Why it makes things fast

Convolving two length-$N$ vectors directly costs $O(N^2)$: every output element is a sum over every
input element. The theorem gives another route:

1. Transform both inputs, $O(N \log N)$ each with the [[Fast Fourier Transform]].
2. Multiply the two spectra elementwise, $O(N)$.
3. Transform back, $O(N \log N)$.

Total $O(N \log N)$. That is the same asymptotic win [[Merge Sort]] gets over insertion sort, and
it is stated in the language of [[Time Complexity]]. It is *the* reason large filters, big-integer
multiplication, and polynomial multiplication all go through the FFT: **multiplying polynomials is
convolving their coefficient vectors**, so the FFT multiplies polynomials in $O(N\log N)$.

## Where the vault already uses convolution

- [[Image Processing]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]: blur, sharpen, and Sobel edge
  detection are convolutions with a $3 \times 3$ kernel. Small kernels are cheaper done directly;
  large ones go through the transform, and this theorem is where the crossover comes from.
- [[Convolutional Neural Network]] and [[CNN]] are named for this operation. The difference there
  is only that the kernel weights are learned rather than designed.
- Filtering in general: multiply the spectrum by a mask that is 1 on the frequencies you keep and
  0 on the ones you do not, then transform back. A low-pass filter is literally that, and it is why
  [[Aliasing]] can be prevented before sampling but never after.

## Related

- [[Fourier Transform]] for the properties table this row belongs to.
- [[Dirac Delta Function]] is the identity for convolution: $f * \delta = f$.
